Wakkerstroom has since become the town where **three separate threads meet**: C.K. Barry the attorney, the George Augustus Kolbe of the gravestones, and the 1901 prisoner. **The Angeline question is now worth more than it was when it was parked.**  ··· **DONE, AND BY ONE SEARCH.** The **Pietermaritzburg estate files** hold 64 Kolbe entries. Both parents’ estates — hers 1923, his 1929 — name **nine children, the daughters under both surnames**. **Gabriel Stephanus** and **Martha Angelina** are alive at both; **Catharina Maria Louisa married a LOUW**; and because Martha Angelina was alive in 1929 she is **neither the Angeline who died at Wakkerstroom in 1900 nor the Volksrust infant of 1901**. rows.what: The phthisis reading on Henry James Booyzen — and both causes were wrong

rows.what: Four archives keep their name pages in four different menu groups
rows.note:
Raised by David on 17 September, looking at two sites side by side: Blažević files **Say Your Name** under **Origins** and Defranceschi files it under **The name**. Measured across the estate, every archive shares a spine — Start, Our line, The families, People & places, Evidence — and beyond it the name pages sit in **five different parents**: *The name* (Defranceschi, Falco, Mazza), *Our line* (Blažević, Booyzen, D'Arcy, Lerena), *Origins* (Blažević), *People & places* (Booyzen's forenames), *People & names* (Luwinski). Blažević's **Origins** group is really about where the family came from — the Bunjevci, the Frontier, the Map, Port Pirie — and the two name pages are lodged there because there was nowhere else to put them. 

**Done 17 September.** The canon is taken from the three archives that already had it rather than invented: **where an archive has two or more name pages they sit in a group called “The name”, between People & places and Evidence.** This archive now has one (The Name, The forenames) and Blažević has one (The Name, The Second Name, Say Your Name) — which also gives **Origins** back to origins: the Bunjevci, the Frontier, what they did, the other emigration, the map, Port Pirie. **Two documented exceptions.** *Lerena* keeps one name page and keeps it under Our line, because a rule that forces a group of one is a rule making work. *D'Arcy* keeps **Fifteen Spellings** in **The Sanigers**, where it is the seventh of ten pages in a narrative about that name; lifting it into a group of two would strand it from the nine pages that give it its point. That one belongs to the D'Arcy session to confirm or overturn.

rows.what: Luwinski's menu spine differs from the other seven and nobody has said whether that is deliberate
rows.note: Found while settling the name group on 17 September. Seven archives run **Start · Our line · The families · People & places · Evidence**. Luwinski runs **Start · Our line · Places · People & names · Evidence** — no families group, places split out on its own, and *People & places* renamed *People & names* to house a single page, **Her names**. It may be right: this archive is one woman and her documents rather than a family, so a families group would be empty and the names question is the whole subject. **But it has never been said out loud**, and a deviation nobody has written down is indistinguishable from drift.

rows.what: Order the two Pietermaritzburg estate files — MSCE 1923 and 1929, Kolbe of Utrecht
rows.note: **The index gave nine children, two deaths and two birthplaces. The files themselves would give more and none has been read.** Elizabeth Johanna du Toit Kolbe, died 12 July 1923 at Saxony, Utrecht; Frederick Fortunatus Kolbe, died 23 November 1929 at Utrecht. A Natal estate file carries a **death notice** — which names the deceased’s own parents, and would say whether Frederik Fortunatus’s father is written as the 1820 Settler. **That single line is what the whole Kolbe descent still rests on inference for.** The files also give husbands’ forenames for the five married daughters, of whom **Louw** is currently a surname and nothing else. **This is a fourth archive building** — NAB, not TAB, KAB or VAB — and it is the same repository the Pietermaritzburg letter has been drafted and unsent for since 12 September. **The letter should now carry these two references.** There are 64 Kolbe entries in that collection and this list names two.

rows.what: Read the DSAB entry on George Augustus Kolbe, and work its source list
rows.note: Melanie Geustyn sent a **second document nobody asked for**: two pages written for the **Dictionary of South African Biography** by **Dr Karel Schoeman**, who worked at the National Library, found in the MSB 751 Background File, **with a list of Bronne (sources)**. It is a secondary work and this archive does not take secondary works as evidence — **but a source list by a historian of Schoeman’s standing is a reading list**, and it is the only one this archive has ever been handed for this man. **Read it, and then work every source in it that is not already here.** **DONE 20 September 2026.** Read in full and set against the archive line by line. It agrees on nine points reached from nine different documents and is wrong about exactly one thing — it makes the Settler’s father a German apothecary, where 121 rate books, two printed masters’ lists, three Gazette notices, the census, the burial register and a sworn Old Bailey deposition all say tailor. **The trade is the son’s, moved one generation up.** It also corrected this archive (MSB 751 is not a letter “on his ordination”), settled the farm name (Wurthemberg = Knapdaar), and handed over nine years of his life this archive did not have — including an accusation, an inquiry and an acquittal in 1836. Its eleven sources are now rows of their own.

rows.what: Thank Melanie Geustyn, and tell her what the letter produced
rows.note: She answered in **twenty-three hours**, sent the manuscript on the **third day**, chased the Background File unasked, and added a **DSAB entry nobody had asked for**. **That is the best service any institution has given this archive.** The reply should say what the letter actually did: it did not carry the address, and it settled the LMS question, dated the obituary, gave Henry his illness, gave Elizabeth a nickname and a city, and turned Charlotte from an inference into a daughter. **It is also worth telling her that the Background File negative was useful** — archivists rarely hear that. The draft is this archive’s; the sending is David’s. **DRAFTED 20 September 2026 — requests/nlsa-thank-you-geustyn.md. The sending is David’s.** It goes as a reply on her own thread, tells her concretely what the four pages settled and what they did not, says that the second attachment corrected this archive, and carries exactly one question, marked optional: the DSAB typescript is unsigned, and the Library is the only body that can say who compiled it and whether it was ever published.

rows.what: The Charles Bell picture of Kolbe at Philippolis, 1834 — found in Edinburgh, original in Johannesburg
rows.note: **FOUND, 20 September 2026, and it is in two countries.** The DSAB sent this archive to the Africana Museum in Johannesburg (now **MuseumAfrica, Newtown**) for a watercolour by **C. Bell** of a church service at Philippolis in 1834 **with Kolbe in the pulpit**, reproduced in *The Journal of Andrew Smith*, ed. Lye (Balkema, 1975). **It is also catalogued in Scotland.** University of Edinburgh, **Centre for the Study of World Christianity, CSWC 60** — five photographs, 1834–1840, *“photograph copies of sketches by the South African artist C. Bell of African congregations”*. **Item 3 is “Mr. Kolbe”, “at Philippolis in 1834”.** The other four are James Archbell, William Edwards, **Jean-Pierre Pellissier** — who is source 9 on the DSAB’s own list — and a service at Ebenezer. **NEXT: ask Edinburgh for a copy of item 3, and MuseumAfrica for the original.** Edinburgh holds a surrogate and is a university archive, which is usually the easier of the two. **This archive holds no likeness of anybody born before 1850.**  **21 SEPTEMBER — MUSEUMAFRICA HAS NO ONLINE CATALOGUE TO SEARCH.** Confirmed that Bell’s originals are there: he made **some 300 watercolours and drawings** on Andrew Smith’s expedition and **a large number of the originals are in the Africana Museum**, now MuseumAfrica in Newtown. **But there is no searchable online collection catalogue**, so the specific Philippolis 1834 sheet cannot be confirmed from here. The museum **published printed catalogues of its Africana**, which is the other route. **Contact: `museumafrica@joburg.org.za`.** **The Edinburgh letter remains the better first move** — CSWC 60 item 3 is catalogued, identified and in a university archive that answers email.  **21 SEPTEMBER — THE MUSEUMAFRICA LETTER IS NOW DRAFTED**, at `requests/museumafrica-bell-philippolis-1834.md`, so both halves of this row are written and both are David's to send. It asks three things in order of usefulness — the accession number, a reproduction and its fee, and where the sheet went if it is not theirs — and it offers the museum the other four names in the series (**Archbell, Edwards, Pellissier, Ebenezer**), because a collection with no online catalogue may file the group under a name that is not Kolbe's. **The Edinburgh letter is still the better first move** and the two should not be sent as a pair: CSWC 60 item 3 is catalogued, identified, and in a university archive that answers email, and if Edinburgh sends the surrogate it will carry details that make the Johannesburg request sharper.

rows.what: Burger Olivier, *So onthou ons die oewerbewoners van ou “Grootrivier”* (Bloemfontein, 1973) — it carries a portrait of him as a young man
rows.note: The DSAB entry says a portrait of Kolbe as a young man was in 1992 held by a descendant, **C.J. du Plessis of Ruigtevlei, district Bethulie**, and that it is reproduced in this book. A privately published Free State local history of 1973 — the kind of book that sits in one or two libraries and nowhere else. **NLSA, the Free State provincial library and Worldcat are the places to look.** If the plate exists, the second question is whether the du Plessis family still has the original. **20 September — the book is identified and no copy is for sale.** Printed by **N.G. Sendingpers, Bloemfontein**; a South African secondhand dealer has listed it, and searches for an available copy return nothing. **The realistic holder is the National Library of South Africa by legal deposit.** Do NOT bolt this onto the thank-you to Melanie Geustyn — that letter already carries two optional questions and a third would be pushing an institution that has been generous. **Ask separately, after she replies.** The deeper route is the other one: the portrait itself was in 1992 with **C.J. du Plessis of Ruigtevlei, district Bethulie**, and a family may still have the original.  **21 SEPTEMBER, SECOND ATTEMPT, AND NO CATALOGUE REACHES IT.** Searched again for holdings: **nothing in WorldCat results, nothing in any library catalogue that surfaces, and no copy for sale.** The publisher is confirmed as **N.G. Sendingpers, Bloemfontein** — a Dutch Reformed Church press — which is consistent with a locally printed 1973 local history that was never widely distributed. **This is not going to be solved from a desk.** The realistic holders are the **National Library of South Africa by legal deposit** and the **Free State provincial library**, and the route is a letter. **Not to be bolted onto the Geustyn thank-you**, which already carries two optional questions.

rows.what: Order the Settler’s death notice — STRUCK: it was ordered and read before this row was written
rows.note: **STRUCK THE SAME DAY IT WAS RAISED.** This row was created from the DSAB source list on the assumption that **MOOC 6/9/35 no. 7698** was a reference this archive did not have. **It has been read since before September.** It is on /documents/ with two photographs and a full transcription: born London, **parents left blank**, aged 42, *Agriculturist*, died 1 December 1844 **“at Knapdaar, in the field cornetcy of Rhenosterberg”**, property about £1000, signed **M. Kolbe** by his widow at Colesberg in January 1845 — **and it names ten children.** **The row was raised because the DSAB write-up was built from the source list without first checking the source list against this archive.** That is the same fault this archive logged on 17 September when a sweep’s results were called new before being checked against what was already held, and the rule written then — *a sweep that returns a name is checked against the archive before it is called a find* — applies to a bibliography exactly as it applies to a name index.

A certificate gives the parish, the witnesses and the signatures, and **Margaret signed the allegation with a mark**. Write to the Albany Museum. **DRAFTED 20 September 2026 — requests/albany-museum-kolbe-marriage-1819.md. The sending is David’s.** To `info@am.org.za`. The Albany Museum keeps **a genealogical archive of the 1820 British Settlers**, which is precisely what he was, so the letter asks a second question as well: whether anything else is filed under **Kolbe** or under **Owen’s party**. **What this archive has of his first four years in the Cape is one sentence in a secondary work.**

rows.what: Schoeman (ed.), *Griqua Records: the Philippolis Captaincy, 1825–1861* — to test the 1836 accusation
rows.note: **Van Riebeeck Society, Second Series no. 25** — 162 official and semi-official documents of the Philippolis Captaincy, including the **Philippolis Law Book** and the correspondence between the Captaincy’s officials and the missionaries. **H. Hendricks, who led the agitation against Kolbe in 1836, was secretary of the Griqua Council** — his papers are exactly what this volume prints. It was published **two years after the DSAB draft was typed**, which is why its own editor could not cite it there. Sold as an eBook by **HIPSA** (hipsa.org.za); no free digitisation found. **This is the one purchase on the whole work list that would test a specific published allegation against a member of this family.**

rows.what: Buy Schoeman (ed.), *Early White Travellers in the Transgariep, 1819–1840* — it prints the 1828 journey
rows.note: **The second document George Augustus Kolbe wrote himself**, and the record of the November 1828 journey to the Caledon valley that the DSAB calls the earliest in the present Free State to survive in writing. **Searched the Internet Archive by title and Google Books; not found.** The Internet Archive holds no run of the LMS *Quarterly Chronicle of Transactions* and the Books API rate-limited the query. Next attempts: the Google Books interface directly, HathiTrust (whose bot check blocked this archive once already), and **the CWM archive at SOAS**, which holds the manuscript journals behind the printed extract and is source 4 on the same list. **20 SEPTEMBER, UNBLOCKED.** The search under KOLBE failed because **the printed version is filed under the other man’s name**. The full citation is “Extracts of the Journal of Messrs Melvill and Kolbe, **addressed to the Rev. Richard Miles, Superintendent of the Society’s Missions in Africa**, Philippolis, **25 Nov. 1828**”, Council for World Missions (LMS) Archives — **which is source 4 on the DSAB’s own list**, two lines above source 6, and the entry never says they are the same document. “An edited version, dated 18 Nov. 1828, appears in **Melvill (1829)**.” **AND THE JOURNEY IS PRINTED IN FULL, IN ENGLISH, IN A BOOK STILL IN THE SHOPS:** Karel Schoeman (ed.), *Early White Travellers in the Transgariep, 1819–1840* (Pretoria: **Protea Book House**, 2003), ISBN 978-1-86919-016-3, **page 30 — “The journey of John Melvill and G.A. Kolbe from Philippolis to the Caledon (1828)”**. About ZAR 285. **It is an edited collection of the travellers’ own texts, so it should carry his account entire.** That is the fourth Schoeman title standing behind one unsigned typescript.

rows.what: Sibree, *A register of missionaries* (LMS, 1923) — found, free, and it holds his whole mission life
rows.note: One printed line would carry his LMS service dates, and this archive now has three to test: **mission assistant 8 February 1828, ordained 25 May 1833, dismissed 19 June 1837.** A register of this kind also records **why** a man left the Society. Not found on the Internet Archive under that title; try Google Books, HathiTrust and the SOAS library catalogue. **DONE 20 September.** **Free PDF, 225 pages, at missiology.org.uk** — this archive had searched the Internet Archive, failed, and written it up as *not found*, which was a negative about one shelf reported as a negative about the world. Entry **278, KOLBE, George Augustus**, gives the whole of his LMS service in eight lines and **settles Mr Miles**: *“accepted provisionally by MR. MILES, Feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the Directors, July 29, 1829”*. It also disagrees with the DSAB draft on the year of acceptance, the day of the ordination and the men who performed it. **And entry 522 makes F.W. Kolbe the Settler’s son, where Schoeman says he was not related.**

rows.what: The 1820 settler roll of the *Nautilus* — read, and both ages are false again
rows.note: The DSAB says the roll gives Kolbe’s occupation as **apothecary** and his age as **20**. He was **seventeen**. **That is the second age this man is known to have overstated** — he had already sworn a false age to marry at sixteen the year before. The roll would also list who else was in **Owen’s party**, which is the company he landed with and a body of people this archive has never looked at. **DONE 20 September.** Nash’s Settler Handbook entry for Owen’s party is published in full at 1820settlers.com. **“KOLBE, George Augustus 20. Chemist. w Margaret 19.”** He was **sixteen**, sailing four days before his seventeenth birthday; she was **sixteen**. **And it does not agree with the marriage allegation eleven months earlier**, where both swore to “twenty-one years and upwards” — nobody twenty-one in January is twenty in December. They were not keeping a story straight; they were telling each paper what it needed. **The party was 52 people, No. 3 on the Colonial Department list**, joint-stock, recruited in London by **Thomas Owen of 9 Carey Street, Horseferry Road, Westminster**, whose father the **Rev J Owen of Fulham** handled the correspondence — and it **collapsed in 1821** when Owen refused to draw rations and left.

rows.what: “Mr Miles” identified — he is the officer who accepted Kolbe, not merely the man who carried the news
rows.note: **An inference this archive is publishing as an inference, and would rather have as a document.** The letter of 23 August 1830 says only *“Mr Miles had called at our house”*. The journal of 25 November 1828 is addressed to **the Rev. RICHARD MILES, Superintendent of the Society’s Missions in Africa**, and Richard Miles — formerly pastor of Brigg in Lincolnshire, originally appointed to Demerara — was sent to Cape Town **to act as Dr Philip’s substitute while Philip was in England**. The office, the continent and the dates all fit: Philip in England from 1826, Miles acting at the Cape in 1828, Philip back and Miles in London by 1830. **What would settle it is the LMS’s own records of its officers** — Sibree’s register, or the CWM home correspondence at SOAS, both already on this list. **If it holds, the man Kolbe reported to from Philippolis is the man who knocked on his father’s door.** **SETTLED 20 September, by Sibree’s register.** *“Accepted provisionally by MR. MILES, Feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the Directors, July 29, 1829.”* **Miles did not carry the news — Miles made the decision.** And the father’s adverb turns out to be the Society’s own vocabulary: provisionally by Miles at the Cape, confirmed by the Directors in London, and a father told his son had been **“fully accepted”**. Richard Miles was Acting Superintendent of the LMS at Cape Town from 1825, standing in for Dr Philip while Philip was in Britain. **The letter still gives no forename, so the surname is carried by the office and the dates — but the office is now his own.**

rows.what: Anne Brest — SENT: stand down from Tuesday, invoice aside, a checked list to follow
rows.note: **URGENT, AND IT IS A PROMISE NOT KEPT RATHER THAN A DISPUTE.** David wrote on 16 September: *“please send the invoice and I will pay it straight away”*. **Invoice No 463 is R11,400 plus R200** and cannot be funded before **Tuesday 22 September**, which is when she drives to Pretoria and for which she has already arranged the files. **The one wrong move is silence.** She volunteered a cap on her own fees before anyone asked, and gave a seventh file free. **Drafted as `requests/anne-brest-payment-and-scope.md`; the sending and the choice are David’s.** It says plainly that the payment will not arrive in time, apologises for having said otherwise, and puts the decision in her hands: **move the visit to a date after payment**, or **keep Tuesday with a reduced set** — Daschner MHG 3734/46, Booyzen MHG 1095/48, and **Kolbe MHG 40293 substituted in, not added**. It also **withdraws the whole of Groups A, B and C** from the 16 September email, so that nothing is being worked that is not on a paid invoice. **Her fees are not the problem and the letter says so.** R2,850 for the first file including the round trip to Pretoria, then by the work done and capped, is a professional day’s rate. **The cost grew because the scope grew** — seven files became twenty-six items in a single reply — and that is this archive’s doing, not hers. **AND THE TIMING WAS NEVER POSSIBLE ANYWAY.** Today is **Sunday 20 September** and the visit is **Tuesday the 22nd**. Her invoice states that **Remitly, Wise and PayPal are not accepted** — it is a SWIFT transfer to First National Bank, and an international transfer from Australia sent on Monday does not land in a South African account on Tuesday; two to five business days is normal. **The visit was never going to be prepaid on this timeline whatever the balance said.** The draft now leads with that, because it is true, it is checkable, and it is nobody’s fault — and it leaves the genuine part of the apology, which is the scope, standing on its own. **20 SEPTEMBER, CORRECTED BY DAVID.** The draft first put **MHG 3734/46 (Daschner)** at the head of the reduced set “for her parents” — which is the reason the original 15 September letter gave. **Her parents are already documented here**, from her baptism at **Barkly Oost, 24 May 1891, entry 120**, and the same is true across that generation: Henry James Booyzen’s 1887 Barkly East baptism names **Willem Hermanus Booÿsen and Catharina Maria Sophia Barry** outright. **The reason had gone and the letter still carried it**, because the list was worked without being checked against the archive — the third time today. **Re-ranked on what is actually missing, which is CHILDREN, not parents:** MHG 40293 (Kolbe, a different question entirely), MHG 769/52 (John Barry — his stone says *aan ons vader* and not one of his children is named here), MHG 5155/51 (Gert Jacobus, from the second marriage, the thinnest branch). **SENT 20 September 2026** (Gmail `1a0bc8e25e24070d`), on David’s instruction and as a reply on her thread. **The two-option letter was abandoned before sending.** David’s judgement was that putting another decision in front of her was the wrong move when the list had already moved four times, and he was right: **the churn was the problem, not the money.** So it asks her to stand down, sets Invoice 463 aside, promises no date, and offers to cover what the short notice has cost her.

rows.what: The Mirror story — FOUND: it is fiction, by James Hogg, and the tailor was right not to believe it
rows.note: **The father devotes two of his four pages to it and asks his son to say whether it is true.** *The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction* ran weekly from 1822 and is digitised in several places. The story: a Scottish colonist near the Xhosa, orang-outangs, a shot young animal that proves to be a chief’s son, a wife carried off, **Capt Johnson** and a company of soldiers, and a recovery after nearly two years. It would date to **1829 or the first half of 1830**. **Worth finding for its own sake**: it is the only thing this archive has that shows what the London household was reading about Africa while its son was living there. **20 September — SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND.** Google Books tried on “Melvill and Kolbe”-style phrasing and on the story’s own terms (“ourang outang” / “orang outang” with *carried off*, *wife*, *colonist*, *Caffre*, *Mirror*, 1829–1830) — **no Books matches at all** — and the same on the open web. **Recorded so nobody repeats it.** Next attempts: the runs of *The Mirror* on Project Gutenberg and the Internet Archive, searched by volume rather than by phrase, and the distinctive surname **Williams or Williamson** with **Capt Johnson**.  **FOUND 21 September, after five failed searches, by downloading the volumes and reading them.** *The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction*, **Volume XIV (1829), pp. 313–318**: **“SPIRIT OF THE PUBLIC JOURNALS — A SINGULAR LETTER FROM SOUTHERN AFRICA. Communicated by Mr. Hogg, the Ettrick Shepherd.”** **It is JAMES HOGG**, author of *The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner*, printed as though it were a settler’s letter home. **Every detail in the 1830 letter is in it**: the chief **KAROO** offering oxen and “a choice virgin to boot” for the settler’s wife; “he foretold I should repent it”; **captain Johnstone** and nine British soldiers; the wife “carried across the river by a band of pongos, (ourang-outangs)”; and her discovery as their **Queen**, with the son taken too. **AND THE ONE DETAIL THE TAILOR GOT WRONG EXPLAINS WHY FIVE SEARCHES FAILED.** He wrote the colonist’s name was “either WILLIAMS, or WILLIAMSON”. **The narrator is anonymous; his son is called WILLIAM.** A man recalling a magazine a year later took the child’s name for the family’s. **Searching for a surname that never existed is why nothing was found** — and the lesson is that a negative built on a detail from memory is a negative about the memory.  **THE METHOD THAT WORKED, for next time:** archive.org serves `https://archive.org/download/<id>/<id>_djvu.txt`. The Mirror volumes are **vol 13 = `s1id13414260`, vol 14 = `s1id13414270`, vol 15 = `s1id13414280`, vol 16 = `s1id13414290`**. Four volumes, 10 MB of text, searched locally in seconds. **Full-text searching a downloaded corpus beats querying somebody else’s index.**  **21 SEPTEMBER, RE-READ AND CORRECTED — AND THE CORRECTION IS THE POINT OF WRITING METHODS DOWN.** This note first recorded the volumes as `s1id134142N0` with suffixes “…260, …270”. **There is no `N0` in the identifier**, and every one of those four ids returns nothing. The prefix is `s1id134142` and the suffix is two digits, not three. **A recipe that will not run is worse than no recipe**, because the next reader spends the time before discovering it. The four ids above were fetched and the story re-read from `s1id13414270` to check every quotation in this row: the heading, the chief **Karoo**, “ten cows and a bull … and a choice virgin to boot”, “he foretold I should repent it”, **captain Johnstone** of the 72nd, the **nine British soldiers**, the wife **Agnes** — married at **Beattock**, which is what makes the colonist Scottish — her son **William**, the **pongos**, and her discovery as the pongos’ **Queen** “sent them … from the country beyond the sun”. **All of it stands, and p. 318 is printed in the text itself.**  **ONE MORE TRAP, worth more than the identifier:** the Gutenberg-sourced copies of the same magazine — the `themirrorofliter…gut` items, one per weekly number — **have no `_djvu.txt` at all**; they hold the Gutenberg file, `<number>-8.txt`. Asking for `_djvu.txt` returns **HTTP 200 and an HTML error page**, which a script that only checks for a non-empty file will count as a success. Twenty-two of twenty-two “downloads” were that page. **Check that what came back is the text before you search it, and treat a zero from an unverified object as no result rather than a negative.**  **The four identifiers above were each fetched and verified on 21 September** at 2.4–2.7 MB apiece, and **the story is in vol 14**. Noted because commit **d3828d3’s message** gave the same thing as a pattern, `s1id134142N0`, **which reads as a literal id and resolves to nothing** — the row is right and the commit message is not, and the commit is not being amended.

rows.what: Mrs Field’s daughter Mary married a Mr Bellew, a surgeon — searched, and not in the index
rows.note: **The first friends of the Soho household to be named anywhere.** Mr & Mrs **Stanhope**; Mr and Mrs **Warner**; **Mrs Field and her daughters**, the eldest of whom, **Miss Mary**, “has married a **Mr Bellew**, a Surgeon, whom I do not know whether you may recollect”. **A surgeon named Bellew marrying a Mary Field about 1829–30 is a findable marriage** — London parish registers and the medical directories both index surgeons. **This archive has had this family entirely through official paper.** These are the people who came to the house. **SEARCHED 20 September, AND NOT FOUND — with a proper control.** Using FindMyPast’s **SpouseLastName** filter (a nonsense spouse returns 0, so the field genuinely restricts): **FIELD × BELLEW returns ONE record in the entire Life Events collection, and it is 1854 at Stepney** — twenty-four years too late, and the letter says she *had already* married by August 1830. Tried as exact spellings **bellew, bellow, ballew, belew, bellewe, bellows**, each against 1823–1835: **all zero**. Widened to **1814–1844: still zero.** **The name variants engine is useless here** — it collapses Bellew into Bell, Boyle and Balow and returns 1,724 rows of noise. **So either the marriage is not in FindMyPast’s London coverage, or the father misheard a surname he was writing from conversation.** Recorded with the spellings tried so nobody repeats them.

rows.what: Frederick William Kolbe — RESOLVED: not the Settler’s son. Sibree is wrong and Schoeman is right
rows.note: **A flat contradiction between two printed authorities, with a chronological impossibility inside it.** Sibree, entry 522: *“KOLBE, Frederick William. Born, Nov. 3, 1821, in South Africa. **SON OF REV. G. A. KOLBE (No. 278)**. Had been connected with the Rhenish Mission… died at Cape Town, Dec. 25, 1899, aged 78.”* Author of an **English–Herero Dictionary** (Juta, 1883), minister at **George** and then **Paarl**. Schoeman: *“F.W. Kolbe (1821–99) van die Rynse Sendinggenootskap **was nie aan hierdie familie verwant nie**.”* Same man, same society, same years. **AND HE CANNOT SIMPLY BE ADOPTED.** Sibree’s 3 November 1821 agrees with his own age at death; the Settler’s known eldest, **John Gerson Eliezar, was born 7 July 1822**, and *his* age at death agrees too. **Eight months apart.** One of the two births is wrong, or one of the men is not who his source says. **Sibree also gives him a sister — CHARLOTTE KOLBE, born 25 December 1829**, who married Rev. William Sykes at Paarl in 1860; the Settler’s 1829 daughter is recorded here under another name. **The paper that would settle it is at SOAS**: a missionary’s own candidate papers state his parentage. **RESOLVED THE SAME DAY.** Three independent works: the **New Catholic Encyclopedia**, on his son Monsignor F.C. Kolbe — “the son of a **WESTPHALIAN (GERMAN) PROTESTANT MISSIONARY** who had married the daughter of a member of the London Missionary Society”; the **S2A3 Biographical Database**, which names him **FRIEDRICH WILHELM KOLBE**, Rhenish missionary and Herero scholar, married at Cape Town in **1849**, at **Okahandja** by April 1850, fled to Otjikango when **Jonker Afrikaner** attacked the Hereros that August, back in the Colony from 1852 — George, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Cape Town; and **DSAB Vol. 5 (HSRC, 1987)**, which carries **its own entry on F.W. Kolbe** and was in print five years before Schoeman wrote. **Sibree’s register has two Kolbes in South Africa, 278 and 522, and a compiler joined them.** The same species of error as Schoeman giving the father the son’s trade. **Charlotte Kolbe, born 25 December 1829, goes with him.**

rows.what: SOAS — the letter is written, with seven exact references including four journals in his own hand
rows.note: **Everything keeps arriving at the same door.** The Council for World Missions / London Missionary Society archive at **SOAS, University of London** holds: (1) **Incoming letters, South Africa** — source 4 on Schoeman’s list, where George Augustus Kolbe’s own reports are; (2) the manuscript of the **1828 journal** with Melvill, source 6, which is the same document under another name; (3) **the letter Dr Philip promised in 1830** to write to him, if it was written; and (4) **the candidate papers of Frederick William Kolbe**, which would say whose son he was and end the contradiction between Sibree and Schoeman. **Four asks, one archive, one letter** — and it is in London, which is the one city on this list somebody could reach. **20 SEPTEMBER — THE CATALOGUE IS ITEM-LEVEL AND EVERYTHING IS FOUND.** Sixty-two records on the surname. **Four journals: CWM/LMS/05/05/100** (Melvill and Kolbe, tour north-east of Philippolis, **13–22 Nov 1828** — the manuscript behind source 6), **/102** (1828–1831), **/106** (1831–1834), **/108** (6 Oct 1832 – Sep 1833). **Incoming correspondence: /044** (1835, and the catalogue names *“George Augustus Kolbe, Philippolis”* among the correspondents), **/046** (1836), and the 1837 file — **1836–1837 is Box 15**, which is the accusation and the dismissal. Drafted as `requests/soas-cwm-kolbe-journals.md`; **the sending is David’s.** `special.collections@soas.ac.uk`, 10 Thornhaugh Street, Russell Square.

rows.what: Three Cape Archives CO references for the Nautilus — and one of them is a signed petition
rows.note: Nash cites three sources for Owen’s party, all at the **Western Cape Archives**, which this archive is already writing to: **CO 6137/1,4** — the list of settlers under Thomas Owen’s direction; **CO 8543** — Special Commissioner **Hayward’s notes**, which is where “this querulous man” comes from; and **CO 3917** — the **Memorial of independent settlers aboard the *Nautilus***. **A memorial is a petition and a petition is signed.** If George Augustus Kolbe signed it he was seventeen, and it would be **the earliest example of his own hand in existence**. Nash also records that **no Agent of Transports’ Return has ever been traced for the *Nautilus***, so these three are the whole documentary basis for the roll. **Add to the standing Western Cape Archives chase.**

rows.what: Dictionary of South African Biography Vol. 5 — and the series was terminated in 1987, five years before Schoeman wrote
rows.note:
Found in S2A3’s source list while resolving the F.W. Kolbe question. **Two reasons to want it.** First, it would give the Rhenish missionary’s parentage and birthplace outright, closing the Sibree error with a named source instead of an inference from three. Second, and larger: **DSAB Vol. 5 was published in 1987 and Schoeman’s G.A. Kolbe draft is dated February 1992**, so the Settler’s entry was written for **a later volume** — and the copy Melanie Geustyn sent is headed *voorlopige teks*. **If the later volumes never appeared, that typescript is the only form the entry exists in**, which is exactly the question the thank-you letter now asks her. 

**21 SEPTEMBER — THE VOLUME IS LOCATED AND IT IS DIGITISED.** *Dictionary of South African Biography* **Volume 5** is on the Internet Archive as **`dictionaryofsout0005unse`** — 978 pages, publisher *Nasional Boekhandel Bpk. for the National Council for Social Research*, which matches. **It is not open full text**: its collections are `inlibrary` and `printdisabled`, so it is a **borrowable** scan. The OCR exists — the text file is **6.09 MB** — and is searchable from inside the reader once borrowed. **So this no longer needs a library building.** A free Internet Archive account borrows it an hour at a time, and the F.W. Kolbe entry can be read and searched there. **A warning about my own first attempt, because it is the fault this archive keeps finding:** fetching the `/stream/.../_djvu.txt` URL returned **an HTML wrapper**, I counted zero occurrences of *Kolbe* in it, and that zero meant nothing whatever — the `<pre>` was empty because the text loads by script. A null from the wrong object is not a null. **Nothing about the entry's contents has been read and nothing is claimed about it.**  **21 SEPTEMBER, LATER — THE SECOND AND LARGER QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND NOT BY BORROWING ANYTHING.** The successor volume says it outright. **E. J. Verwey (ed.), *New Dictionary of South African Biography*, Volume 1 (HSRC Publishers, Pretoria, 1995)** — foreword by **Nelson Mandela**, dated September 1994 — is **openly readable** on the Internet Archive as **`bub_gb_rl8nkyID3WsC`** (`_djvu.txt`, 1.06 MB, collection `americana`). Its Introduction: *“**The decision to terminate the DSAB after the publication of Volume V in 1987** (at that stage 4 518 biographies had been published) **and to embark on the New dictionary of South African biography (NDSAB)** was taken for two reasons — firstly, to adapt to changes in the external environment that seriously reduced the resources available for the continuation of the programme (in fact, threatened its very survival). Secondly, there was a need to reconsider the programme and correct some imbalances.”* **THERE IS NO DSAB VOLUME VI AND THERE NEVER WAS.** **Schoeman's G.A. Kolbe draft is dated February 1992 — five years after the series it was written for had been stopped**, and three years before the replacement appeared. The replacement is not a continuation in the same numbering: NDSAB I carries **129 biographies against the DSAB's average of 900 a volume**, and the Settler is not among them. **So the *voorlopige teks* Melanie Geustyn sent is, on the published record, the only form that entry has ever taken** — which is what the letter asks her, and the archive can now say why it is asking.  **AND THE SAME BOOK PRINTS A CUMULATIVE INDEX TO DSAB VOLUMES I–V, WHICH CORRECTS THIS ROW.** This row assumed one Kolbe entry. **There are three:** **KOLBE, FRIEDRICH CARL — Vol. I, p. 433**; **KOLBE, FRIEDRICH WILHELM — Vol. V, p. 419**; and **KOLBE, FREDERICK FORTUNATUS HOFMEYR — Vol. V, p. 419**. (Separately indexed, and not one of ours: **Kolb(e)(n), Peter — Vol. III, p. 475**, the eighteenth-century Cape writer.) **TWO OF THE THREE ARE ON THE SAME PAGE**, which is how the DSAB sets a family down together — so **page 419 of Volume V is now the single page most worth reading in the whole series**, and one borrowing gets both.  **AND THEN THE FIRST QUESTION ANSWERED ITSELF TOO, WHICH IS THE BETTER RESULT AND THE LESS COMFORTABLE ONE.** This row wanted Volume V because it *“would give the Rhenish missionary's parentage and birthplace outright, closing the Sibree error with a named source”*. **The birthplace is now named without opening the volume, and it rules him out of this family.** **FRIEDRICH WILHELM KOLBE, 1821–1899, was born at GÜTERSLOH in WESTPHALIA and died at CAPE TOWN** (Wikidata Q25615009, resolving both places). He was of the **RHENISH** Missionary Society, married **ISABELLA MARIA ELLIOTT**, daughter of the Rev. William Elliott, at Cape Town in **1849**, went to **Okahandja** in 1850, was driven out by Jonker Afrikaner's attack on the Hereros that August, and came back to the Colony in 1852 — George, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Cape Town (S2A3, entry for **Mrs Isabella Maria Kolbe**, compiled by C. Plug, which cites DSAB Vol. 5 for him). **Their son is Monsignor F. C. Kolbe, 1854–1936**, the theologian and writer. **A GERMAN-BORN WESTPHALIAN OF THE RHENISH SOCIETY IS NOT THE SETTLER'S KIN.** The Settler was born in **Soho in 1802**, son of a Württemberg tailor settled in London, and he was **LMS**. Nineteen years apart, two countries of birth, two societies. **They share a surname and a mission field and nothing else.**  **A LEAD I RAISED AND KILLED WITHIN THE HOUR, WRITTEN DOWN BECAUSE THAT IS THE POINT.** The cumulative index reads, in OCR, *“Kolbe, Frederick **Fortunatus Hofmeyr**, V, 419”* beside *“Kolbe, Friedrich Wilhelm, V, 419”* — and **FORTUNATUS** is a name this archive traces across three families. The Dictionary of African Christian Biography then says Monsignor Kolbe's parents *“were members of the Protestant **London Missionary Society**”*, **and the Settler was LMS**, so for about twenty minutes there was a Fortunatus and an LMS household pointing the same way. **Both halves fail, and my first reading of the index was wrong too.** I took the two entries at p. 419 for **father and son**. **That will not hold**, because the Monsignor is **F. C.** — Frederick Charles — and the index has a **KOLBE, FRIEDRICH CARL at Vol. I, p. 433**, and Volume I (1968) covered people who died before 1950, which he did, in 1936. **The son is very probably the Vol. I entry, not the second Vol. V one**, which leaves the p. 419 pair unexplained and a *Fortunatus* in the index still unaccounted for. What does not depend on any of that: the father is Westphalian and Rhenish; the DACB's LMS is loose — it is the **mother's** father, the Rev. William Elliott, who was LMS — and the DACB also dates the Monsignor **1864** where Wikidata and S2A3 give **1854**. **The Monsignor's own initials are F. C., not F. F. H.**, everywhere he is named by people who knew the family, so the index line is probably two entries run together by the scanner or a name this archive has misread. **A forename and a society are not a descent, and an OCR'd index is not a document.**  **WHAT IS LEFT, AND IT IS SMALLER THAN THIS ROW BEGAN.** Volume V, p. 419 would still confirm F.W. Kolbe's parentage from the printed page and settle what that third index line actually says; **Volume I, p. 433 holds a KOLBE, FRIEDRICH CARL nobody here has accounted for.** Both are borrowable, not open, and borrowing needs a signed-in Internet Archive account, which is not this archive's to create. **That remainder stops at David.** What no longer needs anybody is the question this row was really built on: **the DSAB stopped at five volumes and the Settler's entry was never printed.**

rows.what: Read the four Kolbe journals when they come, and test Schoeman against them
rows.note: **This is the row everything today was pointing at.** Four manuscripts, 1828–1834, in George Augustus Kolbe’s own hand. The sum of his own words in this archive is currently **one sentence, quoted at second hand** through Legassick. When they arrive they will test, from the inside, almost everything this archive has published about him on one source: the Graaff-Reinet years, Boesmanskool and James Clark, the Caledon journey, the move to Philippolis, Melvill’s departure, the ordination, the Berlin Missionary Society at Bethanie — and they may say something about 1836. **They will also be read for what they say about the people among whom he worked**, who appear in this archive so far only as the objects of other men’s sentences.

rows.what: Re-justify all six Pretoria estate files against what the archive now holds, before any of them is paid for
rows.note: **The 15 September brief asked for six death notices “for the parents, the birthplace, the occupation and the list of children”. Since then the Dutch Reformed registers have delivered the parents of that whole generation**, so for several files the stated reason no longer stands. A quick audit: **Henry James Booyzen (MHG 10/57)** has his baptism, marriage, death, burial and a corrected cause — *low*. **Catharina Maria Sophia Daschner (MHG 3734/46)** has her baptism, her husband’s read estate and her grave; what is missing is her **exact death date** and her children in 1946 — *moderate*. **George Downing Mountjoy (MHG 1095/48)** has dates, burial, occupation and marriage; missing is his children — *moderate, and he is in the direct line*. **John Barry (MHG 769/52)** has a gravestone giving 26.4.1884–23.1.1952 and “aan ons vader”, and **not one child named** — *good*. **Gert Jacobus (MHG 5155/51)**, from the second marriage, is the thinnest — *good*. **MHG 52653** is a doubtful reference and expected to fail. **Nothing should be paid for on a reason that has already been answered elsewhere.** **DONE 20 September, and it removed two files from the order.** Each was tested against the free trees, at David’s prompting. **MHG 769/52 (John Barry) — ANSWERED FREE:** FamilySearch **M87R-4X4** gives birth **26 April 1884** and death **23 January 1952 at DELMAS**, matching the Brakpan gravestone to the day, plus a wife **Margritha Maria Susanna Poole (1886–1947)** and **TEN CHILDREN** — the two eldest named **Willem Hermanus** and **Catharina Maria Sophia**, his own parents’ names, which is this family’s documented naming pattern. **MHG 3734/46 (Daschner) — ANSWERED FREE** by her 1891 Barkly Oost baptism, held here. **MHG 5155/51 (Gert Jacobus) — NOT ANSWERED:** FamilySearch G5DK-WZS gives parents only, no death, no spouse, no children. **MHG 1095/48 (George Downing Mountjoy) — NOT ANSWERED and now sharper:** the MyHeritage capture gives his death as **21 February 1947** where this archive has **11 December 1947** from the burial register, with a burial on 14 December. **Only the death notice settles which.** **MHG 40293 (Kolbe 1918) — UNKNOWN:** not found, but **FamilySearch tree search is scored and not filtered** (27,656 and 110,097 results on narrow queries), so absence there proves nothing. **A tree gives names to look for; a death notice gives proof. Two files were buying names this archive can already read for nothing.**

rows.what: The Geni tree tested — and its last unproved name, General Willem Johannes Kolbe, turns out to be published and already here
rows.note: **Twelve names for a household this archive has been unable to name since the Commandant’s obituary was read.** The rule is the one already written for Schoeman’s bibliography: **a list worth working is not a witness.** Nobody is entered here on a tree’s word. **Start with the two that are already half-proved** — Rosa Magdalene Kolbe (1890 Bloemfontein baptism, held) and Maria Margaretha Downing Rousseau (TAB MHG 5450/68, held) — and then **General Willem Johannes Kolbe**, because a general leaves a paper trail a farmer does not. **Beware the name collisions**: this Frederik Fortunatus (b. 1857 Bloemfontein, d. 1930) is a **fourth** man of the name, distinct from the Settler’s tenth child (1839 Bethulie – 1929 Utrecht) and from Frederick Fortunatus Downing Kolbe (d. 1918, TAB MHG 40293). **This archive withdrew a claim within the hour once before over two men sharing a name in one town.**  **21 SEPTEMBER — THE TREE IS HOLDING UP WHERE REGISTERS CAN TEST IT.** Two of the named siblings are now in civil and church registers with McCabe wives: **JAN HENDRIK KOLBE** (m. Rose Maria McCabe, Bloemfontein, 4 June 1872, b. 1849) and **FREDERIK FORTUNATUS** (m. Maria Eliz Petronella Antoinette McCabe). **Jan Hendrik’s eldest son is JOHN GERSON ELIEZER**, the Commandant’s name entire — which is register evidence of the descent the tree asserts. **Still not adopted**; still awaiting VAB MHG M777. **Next from the tree: General Willem Johannes Kolbe, for whom nothing published can be found — ‘General’ may be an honorific.** **21 SEPTEMBER, LATER — THE LAST NAME ON THE TREE IS THE ONE THAT BREAKS IT OPEN, AND HE WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE.** This row asked whether **General Willem Johannes Kolbe** was real or whether ‘General’ was an honorific, because nothing published could be found for him. **He is real, he is published, and the rank is his.** *Afrikanergeskiedenis* (Petronel Fourie) and the Afrikaans Wikipedia both carry him, and behind them stands a printed reference work: **P. J. Nienaber, *Afrikaanse Biografiese Woordeboek* (Voortrekkerpers, 1947), p. 139.** Born **9 July 1847 in the district of PHILIPPOLIS**; led the **Bloemfontein commando**; commanded the southern districts of Bloemfontein; **made general during the siege of Kimberley**; at Paardeberg, Driefontein and the Brandwaterkom; and in **De Wet’s invasion of the Cape Colony in February 1901**. Two horses were shot under him. The French general **de Villebois-Mareuil** praised his leadership; he was liked in his commando. He died in **1941**, aged ninety-four.  **AND THE SAME ARTICLE NAMES HIS HOUSE, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS NOT A NAME MATCH.** **Where the pedigree comes from, stated exactly:** it is set out on the Afrikaans Wikipedia article, which lists two sources and footnotes neither claim to either. **Of the two, only Nienaber can be carrying it** — the *Afrikanergeskiedenis* piece was read here in full and contains no parents, no grandparents and no farm, only the military career. **So the genealogy is Nienaber 1947 by elimination, and has not been read from the page of Nienaber itself.** That matters, and it is why nothing below is adopted. It gives his father as **J. G. E. Kolbe**, his mother as **ANNA JACOBA VAN DER MERWE**, his grandfather as **GEORGE AUGUSTUS KOLBE, a German missionary**, his grandmother as **MARGARET DOWNING**, the grandfather’s place as **Knapdaar, Burgersdorp**, and the home farm as **ONDER-LEEUWBERG in the district of Bloemfontein** — and it says his father was **a commandant in the Basuto war of 1865**. **Every one of those is already held here, independently.** The Commandant’s obituary gives the marriage to Anna Jacoba van der Merwe; the Settler’s obituary gives him as a Londoner of a Württemberg house who named his farm *Wurtemberg*, which is exactly how a 1947 Afrikaans lexicographer would come to call him German; the Burgersdorp stone gives Margaret Downing and Burgersdorp; and **Leeuwberg is the farm the Commandant died on**. **Father, mother, both grandparents, the grandparents' town, the home farm and the father's rank — every one of them already held here, from obituaries and a gravestone, before anybody had heard of this entry.** Two of the agreements are the forenames of women and one is the farm the Commandant died on. **That is a household, not a coincidence of surname.**  **THE MAN WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE AS A NUMBER.** *Williem Johannes Kolbe of Panfontein*, taken prisoner in 1901 aged 54 in the Bloemfontein district, TNA WO 108/368 folio 603 — the right name, the right year of birth, the right district, and captured in the year of the Cape invasion he is published as riding on. **This archive held the General for weeks and did not know it**, because a prisoner-of-war list gives a name, an age and a farm and nothing to hang them on. **Still not entered as the Commandant’s son on Nienaber’s word alone** — but this is a printed biographical dictionary naming four ancestors, not a user tree, and it is a different class of thing from what this row was warning against. **VAB MHG M777 remains the paper that would settle it**, and there is now a second — see the row below on his own memoir.

rows.what: The Kolbe–McCabe “coincidence” — DONE: it is two marriages, not one, and both are in the registers
rows.note: This archive wrote of the 1890 Bloemfontein baptism: *“a second Kolbe–McCabe marriage in the same small Free State world, and this archive does not yet know whether that is a coincidence.”* **The Geni profile suggests it is not.** The Commandant’s widow **Anna Jacoba van der Merwe married Francis McCabe**, Landdrost of Bloemfontein, about April 1871; and her son **Frederik Fortunatus married Maria Petronella Elizabeth Antoinette McCabe**. **Stepmother and daughter-in-law out of the same family.** McCabe died in February 1872 leaving “four sons and two daughters, besides a large family of step-children” — **so the two households were one for eleven months, and a marriage between them afterwards is exactly what one would expect.** WHAT WOULD PROVE IT: the marriage record of Frederik Fortunatus Kolbe and Maria Petronella Elizabeth Antoinetta McCabe, and Francis McCabe’s own estate naming his children.  **ANSWERED 21 September, from civil and church registers rather than trees.** **South Africa, Civil Marriage Records, 1801–1974:** *ANNA JACOBA KOLBE, bride, b. 1825, spouse **FRANCIS McCABE**, Free State, **13 JULY 1871***; and *JAN HENDRIK KOLBE, groom, b. 1849, spouse **ROSE MARIA McCABE**, Bloemfontein, **4 JUNE 1872***. **Free State Dutch Reformed Church Records** carry both couples as parents — Frederik Fortunatus with Maria Eliz Petronella Antoinette McCabe, and John Henry (= Jan Hendrik) with Rosa Maria McCabe, **whose eldest son is named JOHN GERSON ELIEZER**, the Commandant’s name entire. **TWO OF THE COMMANDANT’S SONS MARRIED TWO OF FRANCIS McCABE’S DAUGHTERS.** Two is not a coincidence; it is a stepfamily marrying within itself, out of a household that lasted seven months. **And Jan Hendrik married four months after his stepfather died.** **A DATE THIS ARCHIVE HAD ONLY BY INFERENCE IS NOW WRITTEN DOWN:** the obituary’s “about ten months since” gave April 1871; the register says **13 July 1871**, which is seven. **These are index entries, not images read** — the images would give ages, fathers and witnesses.

rows.what: Margaret Downing’s mother — DONE: both candidate surnames tested and neither survives
rows.note: **The FamilySearch Family Tree gives Margaret Georgina Elizabeth Downing’s parents as JOHN PAUL DOWNING (1765–1839) and MARY KING POOLEY (1768–1834).** This archive has had a father’s name from the tree for a long time and **never a mother at all** — her 1867 Burgersdorp death notice answers the parents question with **“Both dead” and no names**. **FROM A USER TREE AND NOT ADOPTED.** But **“King” carried as a middle name is how a family carries a mother’s maiden name**, exactly as with Mary Ann Maria *Ford* Kolbe, so the name is structured like a real one. **A Downing–Pooley marriage in London in the 1790s would be a document**, and so would a baptism for Margaret in 1803 naming both parents. Look for both. **20 SEPTEMBER, SEARCHED — AND THE PREMISE WOBBLED.** FindMyPast’s Life Events collection holds **exactly one Downing–Pooley marriage before civil registration**: **JOHN DOWNING m. MARY POOLEY, 10 MAY 1802, WELCOMBE (Bishop’s Transcripts), DEVON** — nine months and thirteen days before Margaret’s birth, and in the county this archive’s own tree puts the Downings in (Trick, Heard, Hooper). **But Margaret was born in LONDON, no 1803 London baptism for her can be found, and the two trees disagree about the woman’s surname** — FamilySearch says **Mary King Pooley**, this archive’s own tree says **Mary P King**. **The “P” may be Pooley, or Pooley may be a reading of the “P”.** A candidate, not a finding; nothing adopted.  **CLOSED 21 September.** The single Downing–Pooley marriage in England is **Welcombe, Devon, 10 May 1802**, and that couple **stayed in Devon** — a child baptised there in 1803 and more in 1806, 1809 and 1810, where Margaret was born in London. **Ruled out.** No London baptism exists for her, and that is a real negative because the index covers London well (37 of 100 Smith baptisms in the same window are London). **And the tree’s “Pooley (1768–1834)” is very probably a reconstruction** built from that Devon marriage plus a Mary Downing buried at Welcombe in 1834. **She has no mother, and that is now a tested position.**

rows.what: Two trees give the Commandant’s son two birth years — 1857 and 1859
rows.note: Geni gives **Frederik Fortunatus Kolbe born 22 October 1857 at Bloemfontein**; the FamilySearch Family Tree gives **1859**. Both agree he died in **1930**. **FROM USER TREES, NOT ADOPTED, and the disagreement is the useful part** — it shows the two are **not independent witnesses**. Where collaborative trees agree it may be because one copied the other; where they differ, neither settles anything. **The Bloemfontein baptism register would.** His own children are better documented than he is: **Rosa Magdalena, baptised Bloemfontein 1890**, is already held here.  **21 SEPTEMBER, ATTEMPTED AND BLOCKED BY THE THING IT IS ABOUT.** A record search for *Frederik Fortunatus Kolbe* born 1855–1862 in South Africa returns **the wrong man every time** — the Settler’s tenth child, born 1839 and married to Elizabeth Johanna du Toit, whose eight children this archive already holds. **The name collision is itself the obstacle**, and the date filter does not restrict enough to cut through it. **The Bloemfontein baptism register browsed by year is the way, not a name search.**

rows.what: Test the Welcombe marriage of 10 May 1802 — DONE, and it is ruled out
rows.note: **Three ways to settle it, in order of decisiveness.** (1) **A London baptism for Margaret Georgina Elizabeth Downing in 1803** naming both parents — not found on FindMyPast, so try the London Metropolitan Archives registers and the Westminster sets this archive already used for the Kolbe baptisms. (2) **The Welcombe register itself** rather than the bishop’s transcript — it may give ages, conditions, fathers or witnesses, and the Devon Heritage Centre holds it. (3) **A burial for Mary Downing about 1834**, the year both trees give her. **If the Welcombe couple stayed in Devon, they are not this couple**, and ruling it out is as useful as confirming it. **20 SEPTEMBER, ROUTE (1) TRIED AND IT FAILED FOR A REASON WORTH KNOWING.** No London baptism for Margaret Downing exists in FindMyPast for 1801–1805 — and **after a proper control the nil is real**: of 100 SMITH baptisms in the same window **thirty-seven are London, Middlesex or Westminster**, so the coverage is excellent and the absence means something. **Either she was not baptised in an Anglican London parish, or her family was not a London family** — and the second reading **strengthens Welcombe**, because a couple married in North Devon in May 1802 with a child born in London nine months later and no London kin in the registers is exactly what newly arrived country people look like. Also tested and **failed**: the idea that the surname’s own geography supports Devon. A 160-record sample runs Yorkshire 20, Suffolk 16, Norfolk 16, Cornwall 14, Devon 5 — **Downing is a national name**, and the Devon argument rests only on the tree’s specific ancestry. **RULED OUT THE SAME DAY, by asking whether the couple stayed.** Every Downing record in the parish: 1802 John marriage, **1803 John BAPTISM**, 1806 William, 1809 Emmey, 1810 Elizabeth — **they baptised a child at Welcombe the year after the wedding and kept doing it**, and the Pooleys are equally rooted there. Margaret was born in **London**. **And the 1834 Mary Downing burial in that same parish is almost certainly where the tree’s “Pooley” and its “1834” both came from** — a previous researcher running this identical search and stopping one question earlier.

rows.what: King or Pooley — DONE: neither, on present evidence
rows.note:
**Two user trees, one woman, two surnames.** The FamilySearch Family Tree: **Mary King Pooley (1768–1834)**. The tree this archive was built from: **Mary P King (1768–1834)**. Same years, different surname — which means **at least one of them has parsed a name wrongly**, and it is probably an initial being expanded or a surname being demoted. **FROM USER TREES AND NOT ADOPTED.** The whole Pooley search rests on this being right, so it should be settled before more time goes into it. **The document is Margaret’s 1803 baptism, or her parents’ marriage under either name.** Note that a Downing–KING marriage has not yet been searched at all, and that is the obvious next sweep. **20 SEPTEMBER, ANSWERED IN SUBSTANCE IF NOT IN NAME.** The Welcombe test suggests **neither surname is hers** and that “Pooley (1768–1834)” is a reconstruction built from one Devon marriage and one Devon burial. **So the question is no longer King or Pooley. It is whether either name has any record behind it at all** — and on present evidence neither does. **Margaret Downing has no mother, and that is now a documented position rather than a gap.** 

**Closed 21 September.** The row asked which surname was hers and the answer is **neither, on present evidence** — that is a decision, not a deferral, and the row was still reading *next* while its own note said *ANSWERED IN SUBSTANCE*. Checked before closing: `/documents/#downing-pooley` states the whole of it — the date works to nine months and thirteen days, the county agrees with this archive's own Devon tree without either knowing about the other, **no London baptism exists for her in 1803**, and the two trees cannot agree whether she was a King or a Pooley. `people.json` holds **neither name**, so nothing was adopted. **Margaret Downing has no documented mother, and that is now a published position rather than an open question.** What would reopen it is a document: her 1803 baptism naming both parents, or a Downing–KING marriage, which has still never been swept.  **CLOSED 21 September.** Neither surname survives testing. **Pooley** traces to a Devon couple who never left Devon. **King** returns, on the SpouseLastName filter for 1790–1806, one Norfolk event indexed three times — a *Mary* Downing at King’s Lynn in 1790, wrong person and wrong direction. **The question is no longer which of the two; it is that neither has a record behind it.**

rows.what: Build ONE settled Pretoria list — every item checked against free sources before Anne is asked to price it
rows.note: **This is now owed to somebody.** The letter of 20 September promised Anne Brest *“one list, already checked against what is freely available, so that everything on it is something only the archive can answer”*. **That promise is the whole reason her Tuesday was cancelled, and it has to be kept properly or not made again.** **The method, which should have been applied from the start:** for every reference, state what is actually missing; search FamilySearch’s tree, Geni and the MyHeritage capture for it; and keep the item **only if those come back empty or only if a document is needed to prove what a tree merely asserts** — and say which of the two it is. **The three that survive so far are TAB MHG 40293 (Kolbe, 1918), MHG 5155/51 (Gert Jacobus) and MHG 1095/48 (George Downing Mountjoy, whose death date the tree and the burial register disagree about).** **The nineteen items of Groups A, B and C have never been through this at all** — seven WLD court files, five Lerena items, the OD signatures, the CJC Marico claim, SAB VWR 2. **None of them goes back on a list until it has been.** **DONE 20 September — and it lives on /errands/, not in a note file.** The Pretoria entry there was already the right structure and was **stale in exactly the predicted way**: it still called the Daschner notice *“the most wanted page in this list”* for parents this archive had held for a fortnight. **Rebuilt in three tiers.** (1) **The three death notices that survived the check**, each labelled with why — MHG 40293 (untested, because FamilySearch tree search is scored not filtered), MHG 5155/51 (the tree has parents only, nothing else), MHG 1095/48 (kept for a NEW reason: the tree says he died 21 February 1947 and the burial register says 11 December, and only the notice settles it). (2) **The items no tree could ever answer** — the WLD divorce, the seven CJC Marico claims, the two OD school files wanted for a signature, SAB VWR 2, and the David Schalk index search. These were never candidates for the test. (3) **Dropped, with reasons, so nobody orders them again** — MHG 3734/46, MHG 769/52, MHG 10/57 and MHG 2703/63. **MHG 52653 was reclassified from a file to an index question**: ten minutes at a counter for the correct reference, not an hour in a strongroom. **Groups B and C were not audited and are not on it** — Wear, Longhurst and Rogue Luis Lerena return zero hits in this archive's people, so they belong to the Wear research and the Lerena archive and need their own owner.

rows.what: Groups B and C need an owner — twelve Pretoria items that are not this archive’s to audit
rows.note: **They were on the order to Anne Brest and they were never checked, because this archive cannot check them.** **Wear**, **Longhurst** and **Rogue Luis Lerena** return **zero hits** in `people.js`; Nuno Fernando Lerena has one line. **Group B** is seven items — WLD 2026/1951, 2960/1962, 185/1949, 790/1957, 978/1960, 2225/1953 and MHG 3632/50 — and belongs to the **Wear/Luwinski research**. **Group C** is five — TPD 1367/1980, 1248/1979, MHG 1518/73, 6746/71, WLD 8043/77 — and belongs to the **Lerena archive**, which is a sibling site with the same method. **Most of them are court files and wills, which no family tree holds**, so they would very likely survive the same test that cut this archive's list in half — but **somebody who holds those families has to run it**, and it should be run before they go back on any invoice. **The promise made to Anne was one checked list; a list half-checked is not that.**

rows.what: All seven errand entries audited for staleness — four were out of date
rows.note: **/errands/ is the page somebody standing at a door reads, so a stale entry there wastes a journey rather than a search.** All seven audited on 20 September. **PRETORIA** — rebuilt entirely; it still called the Daschner notice “the most wanted page in this list” for parents held here a fortnight. **WESTERN CAPE** — still asked somebody to stand at a door for **MSB 751**, answered by the National Library on 18 September; marked answered with the result recorded rather than deleted, because an errand that quietly vanishes teaches nothing. **KEW** — said “not yet written to” when the letter has been written and corrected twice, and asked for “WO 12” when the piece is now **WO 12/1450** and the window four quarters wide, because the regiment left the Cape in **September 1817** and not 1816. **BARKLY EAST** — the Indwe index has since been read and the entry did not say so; sharpened to record what it gave and what only the originals will. **GRAHAMSTOWN** — gained a second institution: the **Albany Museum**, which has held a photocopy of the 1819 Kolbe–Downing marriage certificate since before 1992. **PIETERMARITZBURG and BLOEMFONTEIN** were current; Bloemfontein’s C129 was sharpened instead, because it is now the document that would prove a stepbrother married a stepsister.

rows.what: Württemberg before 1792 — the tailor’s marriage is probably not in England
rows.note: **The negative is now controlled and it points abroad.** No Kolbe–Larman marriage exists in FindMyPast in either direction, with a working control; and the index demonstrably reaches this family’s own parish, because it holds the **1810 Kohlbeck banns at St Anne’s Soho**. **The German Lutheran register is ruled out by statute** — Hardwicke’s Act of 1753 required an Anglican ceremony for validity, with exemptions only for Quakers and Jews. **So: an unindexed English parish, a wrong surname, or a marriage abroad.** He was born in **Württemberg in 1765**, entered his birth county as **“FOREIGN”** in the 1841 census, and the first child of the house was baptised in London in **1792**, when he was twenty-seven. **The gap between birth and first baptism is twenty-seven years and this archive has nothing in it.** **Where to look:** the Württemberg church registers, which are well digitised — FamilySearch and Archion both hold them — and the family tree’s own claim of a line back to a Johann Gottlieb Kolbe of 1699 and Maria Barbara Jung, which is tree-only and untested and would give a parish to start in. **A marriage abroad would also explain why no English record has ever been found for a man this archive can otherwise follow through 121 rate books.**  **21 SEPTEMBER, FIRST PASS WORKED.** **FindMyPast is the wrong tool and that is worth writing down:** it indexes *Württemberg* almost entirely as a **birthplace field in emigration records** — American naturalisation petitions, passenger lists, English censuses — not as German parish registers. `Kolbe` + Württemberg returns **0** there against a working control. **FamilySearch is the right tool and it half-answers.** Its *Germany, Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages and Burials, 1500–1971* and *Germany, Deaths and Burials, 1582–1958* **do reach Württemberg, and Kolbes are plainly there** — Albershausen, Altdorf (Nürtingen), Knittlingen (Maulbronn), Sulz, Eltingen (Leonberg), across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. **So the family tree’s “Württemberg” is at least a plausible region, which it had never been shown to be.** **But there is no Gottlieb or Gottlob Kolbe indexed in Württemberg at all** — three results, none relevant. **THE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS: this is a search of an INDEX, not of the registers.** Much of the Württemberg church-book material on FamilySearch is browse-only images, and Archion holds the rest behind a subscription. **NEXT: the named parishes above, browsed, and Archion.** Noted in passing: a **Carl Gottfried Kolbe buried at Sulz, Württemberg, 10 September 1787, born 1736** — the tree gives the Settler’s grandfather as born 1736. Wrong forename, wrong death year, right decade and region. **Not a match and not adopted.**  **21 SEPTEMBER, SECOND PASS — THE FINDMYPAST NEGATIVE IS WITHDRAWN AND REPLACED WITH A NARROWER ONE.** The claim above that FindMyPast indexes Württemberg only as an emigration birthplace is **wrong**, and the correction is logged. FindMyPast holds ***Germany Marriage Index 1558–1929***, a real German marriage index with **338 Kolbe marriages**, giving both parties, the year and the parish — **and it reaches Württemberg**: Grötzingen, Schwarzwaldkreis 1685 and **Knittlingen, Neckar 1741**, which is one of the very parishes the first pass named. **The 0 came from a place filter that returns 0 to everything**, including `westfalen` when seven of eleven records in the window are Westphalian. **WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE NOW:** all **eleven** Kolbe marriages in the index between **1778 and 1798** were read, and **none is a Gottlieb and none is in Württemberg** — the window's coverage is entirely Prussian, Pomerania to the Rhineland. **So the index cannot answer this question in this period, rather than answering it in the negative.** **NEXT, AND UNCHANGED:** the named parishes browsed on FamilySearch's images, and Archion. **But the search is one step less blind**: Knittlingen is now a parish where Kolbes demonstrably married, and it is on the first-pass list for independent reasons.  **AND THERE IS NOW A NAMED COLLECTION TO READ, WHICH THERE WAS NOT THIS MORNING.** ***Germany Birth and Baptism Index 1558–1898*** on FindMyPast holds **952 Kolbe entries**, and a baptism entry gives **the parish and the parents** — which is exactly what is missing for the twenty-seven years between his birth in 1765 and the first London baptism in 1792. **The 952 have NOT been read** and nothing is claimed about them; FindMyPast stopped rendering after a run of rapid queries and the reading is the next session's. **Two traps to carry into it, both measured:** the **place filter on these German sets returns 0 to everything**, including places printed in its own results, so the 952 must be sorted by eye and not filtered; and **`datasetname` and the year filters annihilate each other** — 952 alone, 0 with a year added, while `sourcecategory=parish baptisms` with the same year works and returns 619. **Filter by category and year, then read the record set off each row.**

rows.what: I said four archives were ready for a second map layer. I had counted files, not read them.
rows.note:
The kit's Atlas gained a `schemes` prop on 20 September so an archive can ask more than one question of the same ground, and the case made for it was that **D'Arcy, Blažević, Falco and Mazza already hold the data**. **They do not.** Read properly: D'Arcy's 89 graves are keyed to *cemeteries with plot references* — “Lutwyche Cemetery, Brisbane (Port. GP5, Sect. 42A, Grave 78)” — and **18 of them match an atlas place**; Blažević 33 of 72; Mazza **0 of 10**. The coverage files are not geographic at all: Blažević's is per-person (ahnentafel, read/unread), D'Arcy's is per-database (FreeREG, Bristol, verdict *unusable*), Falco's is per-document (87 register acts), and Lerena's *film map* is a map of a **film reel**, thumbnail luminance against a threshold of 60, with no place in it. **Nothing here is a place layer without a cemetery-to-town mapping or a geocode, and that is each archive's editorial work, not something to derive from outside.** The mechanism is ready and unused; what each archive needs to supply is `cats: {scheme: cat}` on its own atlas rows. The claim was made from a file listing and should have been made from the files. 

**Closed 21 September: the recording was the deliverable.** This row has no action left in it — it exists so that a claim I made to the estate, and which was wrong, is written down beside the numbers that disprove it. The mechanism it describes is shipped and the four archives know what they would have to supply. **Leaving a correction open as though it were work makes the list longer and the record no truer.**

rows.what: Taking Defranceschi's map off its MutationObserver is a rewrite, not a removal
rows.note: Offered as a next step and withdrawn on reading the component. `AtlasTimelineTint.astro` is 1,220 lines and **the scheme switch is the smallest thing in it**. It also carries: the panel's coverage-timeline tinting (gap rows, soft gaps, films, records, folds); `startOff`, which clicks the kit's own buttons after its first `apply()` because the kit keeps its filter state in a closure; **the whole view in the address bar** — `?layers=people,graves&base=terrain&q=Senj`, so a view is a link somebody can send; a **basemap switcher**; full screen; and a responsive rebuild of the controls. Ripping out the scheme half would remove a fifth of it and put the other four fifths at risk for no gain, **because the kit cannot yet do URL state, basemaps or full screen**. The sequence is the other way round: the kit absorbs those three — all of which the Record Atlas has independently invented too — and the local component then shrinks to the panel tinting that is genuinely this archive's.

rows.what: The Record Atlas already holds every place the family shelf layer holds — all 1,239 of them
rows.owner: David, and the Geneology Map session
rows.note: Measured 20 September. **The Record Atlas** (`TheMap`, the standalone product) holds **9,472 places and 3,504 collections**, with every name a place has ever had, who holds the paper, what it costs to look, and whose empire filed it. Defranceschi's map carries a *shelf* layer of **1,245 parishes** — how far this family has got with the registers. **1,239 of those 1,245, or 100%, are already in the Record Atlas.** Its other layers are not: people 72 of 165, graves 18 of 64, records 16 of 31, because those are about a family and the shelf is about records. **That is the division of labour, and it is already true in the data.** The global question — where are the records, who holds them, can I see anything tonight — belongs to the Record Atlas; a family archive should ask where it can put a named person, where the graves are, and what it has read, and **link out for the shelf rather than keep a second copy of it**. The Record Atlas's own component says it descends from the family Atlas and names three things it does better: colour by what a stranger can open rather than by how far one researcher has got, a year that filters rather than decorates, and a panel that fetches so the index stays 145 KB instead of 2.5 MB. **It is the most evolved of the three maps in this estate and it is the one nothing else shares code with.**
